intro.text: This document lists what the game lets you choose and what it keeps track of, visible or hidden, taken directly from the game’s code. Numbers are the values in the code today. “Hidden” means the game never shows the number: you see words, ranges or the results.

blocks.text: Settings you choose on the start page

items: Difficulty:

Regular guy (The full game. Most careers peak in the 60s and 70s; the NBA is common, stardom is earned.) · Reality hits hard (Like real life: most careers end short of the NBA, and those who make it fight for a spot. Every choice counts.) · Shoot for the stars (Built for greatness: every career reaches stardom, and the very top is within reach.)
Fast break (switch):

quick seasons with one tap; every real decision still stops the game, a press conference is one answer, and every tab folds its extra cards behind one button. Growth is a little faster to make up for the skipped choices.
Sim mode (switch):

fast break plus the calls made for him: the routine ones (the season plan, the summer, national team call-ups, G League assignments, press conferences, answered humbly) and the turning points, where it takes the first choice that is not high risk. Home lists each turning point it decided since the last move, with how it went, like the card of a call he made himself; the list clears with his next move. It stops for offers, the draft, contracts, brands and storylines. Four ways of choosing turning points were played over 300 sim careers each and all landed within noise (mean peak 69.9 to 70.4, standard error about 0.65); this one is the closest to the balance harness’s smart player. Since round 35 (owner: “sim mode should be unlocked once the user completes one full round (until retirement) of each difficulty”) the switch opens only once the device has a career finished with an NBA All-Star team at Regular guy, Reality hits hard and Shoot for the stars (owner: “lets go with allstar as the requirement”); a Comet does not count. Until then the chip is grey and says which difficulties are still to go; a career saved with Sim on can still switch it off.
Simple text (switch):
every explanation on every tab is hidden; status lines and a press answer’s tone stay.
Built in a lab (mode):
design a player and spend credits on ratings instead of training (also a mini-game).
Name and jersey number (0–99), dominant hand (left or right), country, hometown and high school (assigned when not chosen).
Position:
PG (Point guard), SG (Shooting guard), SF (Small forward), PF (Power forward), C (Center). Random never repeats the last pick.
Archetype:
five per position (25 in all), each a starting shape of the eight ratings that adds up to the same total.
Focus stats:
two ratings that grow about 1.8 times faster (the rest at 0.85). Changing them later needs a breakthrough season.
Height:
a full-grown height is drawn for the position (below); a young player sees only a projection that can miss by several inches.

items: Rough Road (with Reality hits hard):

picking Reality hits hard asks once whether to take the hardest way to play (flags.oath). Take it and the road picks the player at random: position, archetype, focus ratings, hand, country (by real-world odds), name, number and his look (skin, hair, face: the page warns that the avatar is rolled too), shown on the last step with no reroll. Then master mode is on, and Fast break, Sim mode and undo are locked off for the whole career (the engine refuses the first two). Simple text is allowed. The honour: the mark in the top bar, a leaderboard of its own (it counts on Reality’s too), the Reality 99 hall and the career log; six achievements of its own; an iron-and-red banner on the retirement page; a resolute sound when it is taken.
Comet (with Shoot for the stars):

Shoot for the stars at hyper speed, about five minutes a career (flags.comet). Fast break and Sim mode are locked on for the whole career. On top of sim the game takes the youth academy’s call and never stops between seasons; he keeps where he plays, the draft, brand deals and when to retire. Draft night, award nights, finals, breakthrough seasons, storyline chapters, the nickname and its logo keep a page of their own; college commitments, tournaments and injuries go into a list of highlights on Home (On the way here). The honour: the Comet mark in the top bar and on the career log, a leaderboard of its own (it leaves the Shoot for the stars board to careers played by hand), no undo; four achievements (Shooting Star, Light Speed, Tail of Fire, Hall of Comets); a comet’s sound when it is taken.
Comet’s playtime:

scripts/playtime.ts plays careers the way the game does and prices what reaches the screen: creating the player 75 s; team offers 12 s, the draft 8 s, a brand deal 6 s, retiring 6 s, any other decision 8 s; a stop between seasons 8 s; a story page 6 s; a list on Home 4 s; the end of the career 30 s. Comet over 1,000 careers: mean 5.1875 minutes (SD 0.6977), median 5.1167, 80% between 4.3167 and 6.0833; Shoot for the stars with plain sim about 7.86. Comet’s mean peak (87.94) matches plain sim’s (88.22). The prices are estimates, not timed with players.

blocks.text: On the identity step the player picks his look from the same parts every avatar in the game is built from: one of seven skin tones, a hairstyle (13), a hair colour (5) and facial hair (7), shown live on his sprite in a plain white or black jersey with his number and nothing else. He starts with no accessories; the wardrobe adds what he buys. The look is kept with the career (player.look) and its career card, and every picture of him uses it. Random, and Rough Road, roll it like the rest.

Owner, round 36: “filter out curse words or non english characters in the player name”. A player’s name keeps letters A to Z, spaces, apostrophes, hyphens and dots, up to 28 characters; accents become plain letters as they are typed (Jokanović is Jokanovic, Traoré is Traore) and other alphabets, numbers and emoji drop. Swear words and slurs are refused, also spelled with numbers (b1tch) or spaced out (F u c k), and Next stays off until the name is clean; real names that only look close stand (Hancock, Dickerson, Sexton, Cumberland, Assane). The list lives encoded in src/content/blocked.ts, in three parts: words refused anywhere, stems refused at a word’s start, and words refused only on their own. All 9,216 names the game picks at random pass (a test checks every one).

chapters.title: 2. The road map: the tutorial, and what the rest opens

blocks.text: Every device starts here, whatever it has saved (owner: “anyone who goes into the browser automatically gets assigned to the tutorial, regardless of their data”). Since round 35 the tutorial is the beginner level alone (owner: “make only the beginner level of tutorial necessary. once the user graduates from it, they get the key and gain access to the main game”): graduation follows it and opens the full game with Regular guy. It keeps to the essentials (owner: “there are still too much features accessible in the tutorial mode”): Home without the milestones or the fan talk, and a Player tab of ratings and status only. The road map’s other stops each open a part of the game: intermediate opens Reality hits hard, advanced Shoot for the stars, the island the mini-games (owner: “lock the other difficulties ... except for regular guy. also lock minigame”). Saved careers wait untouched.

Measured with the playtime model and the smart player, 200 careers a level. Every level starts on the first page of a high school senior season (the first three years are played for him with plain, safe calls) and ends when its NBA seasons are played. The goal is an NBA All-Star team (owner: “nba all star could be achieved above 80%. make that the goal”); reached or not, the level is passed, and a missed goal has an ending card of its own with a sad loop before the thank-you page.

items: Beginner:

the Home and Player tabs; six plans, one a season at full strength (balanced, grind, shooting, strength, playmaking, defense); one turning point a season from a set list, each teaching one thing (the risk tag, fame, a role, form, injury risk, mood, coach trust); three things in the shop and one purchase; one last shot in his first NBA playoff game, down one with the ball if the game was not already close. American, with colleges and NBA teams calling only; no contract talks.
Intermediate:

adds the Season tab, the archetype and focus steps, choosing among offers, all twelve plans once a season (one or two), playable playoff games, contract talks on the first NBA deal past the rookie scale, a nickname, brand deals, a rival and the fast break switch.
Advanced:

adds the country and the shooting hand, the roads abroad (the G League and overseas offers), plans for each half, storylines, staff, the head coach, team style, trades, the starting five, crunch time, the body map and weight, and sim.
Never in a level:
press conferences, the locker room, duos, the farewell tour, the record watch, Love and the next generation, the ring chase, the national team and Around the league; the closing tour shows them.
Pace:
every level plays at fast break’s pace but keeps its own plans, its shop and, from intermediate on, its playable playoff games. Without it, intermediate took about 15 minutes and advanced about 20.
Offers:
below advanced only colleges and NBA teams call; if nobody else does, the G League, and if not even that, anyone, so a career is never stuck.

one mode a stop; the exit code opens what beginner does; a device that finished the old tutorial keeps everything (the road’s first load since round 35 sets a version, and a device already free gets all); multiplayer is Regular guy, so it is open to everyone who graduates.

The dev deck:
everything is open unless a card previews the tutorial.

blocks.text: Every mini-game once with a C or better, any time between levels (owner: “they must play each minigame at least once, earning at least a C”); the marks follow each game’s career-bonus tiers, and the best grade in each is kept. The boat leaves from the dock on the map.

104 lessons: beginner 31 (21 to read, 10 to do), intermediate 21 (14 and 7), advanced 24 (19 and 5), the closing tour 27 (18 and 9) and one after graduation. One at a time: the page is shaded but for one control; a lesson to read waits for Got it (Enter or Space), a lesson to do counts only a real control used inside the highlighted one, and other keys are blocked. None can be skipped (owner: “the guide steps are unskippable”): the exit code is the only way out, and every note offers it.

24 stops after the levels, each a real career played by the dev deck’s player until the moment it needs. Nine for what no level has (a star in his prime, a duo, a press conference, the record watch, the national team, love, the farewell tour, chasing a ring, the next generation); fourteen to catch up whatever the player’s own levels never showed (the offseason’s moves, the Player and Season tabs, the bracket, offers, a storyline, a brand deal, the summer program, a turning point, a playoff game, crunch time, the last shot, the last minutes of a final, sim mode); the tabs and the switches last. A stop whose lessons are all done is skipped. Next stop waits until a stop’s lessons are done.

items: Graduation:

after the beginner level, a pixel diploma lists the road’s stops and what each opens, and shows the exit code with a copy button; Open the full game frees the device and opens the start page with Regular guy recommended (owner: “highly suggested, but not necessary”).
The exit code:

Skip tutorial, at the top of every tutorial page, and floating above a lesson’s shade while one is up (round 35, owner: “let users skip mid tutorial”), takes it (owner: “this allows old users to skip”); it opens what beginner does. It is checked against a hash; the game holds it only lightly encoded because the graduation page has to show it, and a test keeps it from appearing as plain text in the source.
For good:
once the tutorial is finished or the code entered, the device stays free (the owner’s call at the end of the round).
The plane:

graduation’s last button is Take the plane to the main land, under a card with the plane on the island’s airstrip. The flight is five seconds in steps of twelve frames a second (wheels up from the road map’s island, over the sea, down on the main land’s runway), a caption for each part, the engines spooling up and the tyres and the cabin bell at touchdown. Skip, Enter or Escape lands at once. It plays once on a device (btr-plane-seen) and never with reduced motion; the dev deck always shows it. The main land’s airport flies back to the road map the same way.

blocks.text: A level career and a closing-tour career have no save slot, career log card, achievements or leaderboard post. A level career in progress has one save of its own, so a reload resumes it, and it cannot be retired early (owner: “they also cant quit”). Simple text, Master mode and Guide mode are off in a level and come back as they were.
On screen and in the ear

items: The road map:

a 192 × 108 pixel map: the high school, the college, the NBA arena, the closing tour’s stage (a backdrop with a gold star, a plank floor and light towers), the road between them and an island across the sea. His car, in his look, drives on to the next stop the first time the page opens after a level; a boat takes him to the island. The bucket list is a chunky pixel scroll (owner: “a more paper vibe ... more roughly pixellated”).
Cards that pop out (owner:

“instead of putting the cards bellow the map, make it so that when the user clicks on the buildings, or use the arrow keys to move around, the cards pop out”): the map opens clear, with a pixel pin on every place (done, next, open or locked; the next one hops). Clicking a place, or driving to it with the arrow keys, pops its card out beside it; Enter opens the card of the place the car is at, Escape folds it away. On a phone the card sits under the map.
Each level’s place:

cropped from the map onto the level’s start page, its stop on the road map and its end card; intermediate and advanced show what they add as pixel icons with a word or two (owner: “use a lot of icons and little text”). Graduation has a mortarboard.
Sound:

Road trip (128 bpm) on the road map and level pages, So close (76 bpm) on a missed goal; the car’s engine, the boat’s horn, a pencil tick for a lesson done and a fanfare at graduation. The two loops count toward no music achievement.
Back on the road map:

once the full game is open, picking Regular guy on the start page pops out a card (“Back on the road map?”) that opens it, to play any level again (owner: “put the levels (tutorial) card on the main page as a pop out challenge for regular”).

chapters.title: 3. How the game decides: the main logic

blocks.text: A plain-language tour of the rules behind the results. Only the main factors are here; every exact number lives in the game’s balance file. Worked examples are given to 6–7 significant figures.

items: Every team has a strength number:
the quality of its roster plus its coach.
The stronger team wins more often, never always:
win chance = logistic((your strength − their strength + home edge) ÷ 4.5). Home court is worth 1.2 strength.
He changes it:
(his OVR − the OVR of the player he replaces) × (his share of the minutes) × 0.25. An 85 OVR starter replacing a 75, playing 36 of 48 minutes, adds 1.875 strength.
Extras add or take away strength:

chemistry, coach trust, star gravity (OVR 84 and up), the winning-player edge (great defenders, floor generals, 3&D), team style, roster fit, the duo or Big Three, the fans, the city, storylines and midseason swings.
Playoffs are series:
best of seven, game by game, with the same win chance. A small edge per game becomes a big edge per series.
A title is four series in a row,
so the per-game edge is multiplied four times over.
The playoff grind:
in NBA playoff games his team gives up 1.0 strength (every opponent raises its game). At even strength that turns 50% into 44.46719%.
Playoff-only extras:
some fans (playoff edge) and winning players (the edge counts 1.6 times in the playoffs) help more in May and June.

head: Chance to win each game
Chance to win a series
Chance to win four series (the title)

blocks.text: This is why a title needs a strong team around him, not only a great player: one point of strength moves the title odds far more than one point of OVR does on its own.
Roster fit: how the players around him fit together

items: Every teammate gets ratings:
his archetype’s leanings around his OVR (85% of the archetype’s shape, a little noise of his own), shifted so they still add up to his OVR.
The team profile:
the average of each of the eight ratings, the starting five (him included) counting three times the bench (the next four players).
Balanced:
how evenly the profile is spread. A spread (standard deviation) of 3.4 rating points is neutral; 1 point less is fully balanced (+1), 1 point more fully lopsided (−1).
Built for the system:
every team has a system (its coach’s, or the style he sets). The lean of the profile toward the ratings that system wants, ÷ 2.5, from −1 to +1.
Shape = the better of the two,
minus 0.33 (the average of that better score, so an average roster adds nothing), × 0.8 strength.
Depth:
his bench’s average OVR against the league’s usual bench, ÷ 3.5, from −1 to +1, × 0.5 strength.
Then the difficulty’s team-factor dial:
Regular guy ×0.5 (never below 0.5), the other modes ×1.

blocks.text: Measured over 1,100 seasons of simulated careers: the profile’s spread was 2.46 (10th percentile), 3.40 (median) and 4.46 (90th); the lean toward the system −2.86 to 2.22; the bench gap −3.44 to 3.78. The resulting bonus at full dial averages +0.025388, with 10% of seasons below −0.724839 and 10% above +0.759937. Worked example: a balanced five (spread 2.9, balance +0.5) with a bench 2.1 OVR above the usual one (depth +0.6) gets (0.5 − 0.33) × 0.8 + 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.436 strength, or 0.218 in Regular guy.

items: Ratings set what he is good at;
minutes and role set how much he gets to show it.
Each game has form:
a hot or cold night (about ±17%) and a streaky rhythm across the half; morale nudges it.
Value per game
(the number the awards use) = points + 1.05 × rebounds + 1.55 × assists + 2.3 × (steals + blocks) − turnovers, plus a bonus for scoring efficiently.

blocks.text: The bar for All-Star and MVP

Owner, round 36: “instead of reducing growth too much, let’s set the bar a bit higher”. He makes an All-Star team only from his conference’s top six (the tutorial levels keep the top twelve, so a level’s All-Star goal stays reachable), and the MVP voters take 6 points off his score and 2.5 more for each MVP he has won (MVP_BAR; the live ladder too). Generated players are judged as before.

items: Age sets the base speed:
fastest at 14–18, slowing through the 20s, nothing left at 34. Early and late bloomers shift the curve.
Potential is the ceiling:
the closer a rating is to it, the slower it grows.
Focus ratings grow 1.8 times as fast;
the others 0.85 times.
The hidden growth rate
(about 0.5 to 2.2) multiplies everything; fast learners also break through and surge more.
Each half:
the plan, minutes, how well he played, mood and the half’s outcome (surge, breakthrough, steady, plateau, setback) multiply it.
Regular guy only:
above OVR 85 growth slows by 7% a point (never below 40%), so the very top takes work.
Aging that diverges:

owner, round 36: “many legendary players were still elite at their mid 30s”. Past an 82 peak, each point of peak OVR slows the yearly decline by 4%, down to 40% of it; a durable body starts declining at 32 instead of 31; the age ceiling is 90 at 37, falling 1.7 a year (about 85 at 40, 68 at 50). The league’s generated players age as before. Regular guy careers that never retire by choice with a 95+ peak average 95.2 at 35, 90.9 at 38, 87.5 at 40 and 73.5 at 48; a peak in the 70s ages as before (about 64.5 at 35).
Two career changers, both extremely rare:

the next step (25 to 33, once a career, 0.15% a summer: +7 to +11 on every rating, a ceiling 6 to 12 higher, faster growth; about 1.3% of Regular guy careers) and the career-altering injury (a torn ACL, meniscus and MCL, 0.06% a summer: one season out, or two in 40%; athleticism −18 to −26, finishing, perimeter defence, rebounding and interior defence −8 to −13, the rest −3 to −6, every ceiling −8 to −14, potential −10 to −16; about 1.5% of careers). The leap belongs to 19 to 24.
The top of Regular guy’s curve:

owner, round 37: “i want the upper hand (above 70 ovr) to go linearly down ... aim the more niche factors than the main factors”. A rating pushed past its cap by a turning point, the shop or a mini-game settles back each summer by a share of the excess: nothing at OVR 76, rising in a straight line to all of it at 98 (settleBack, player/growth.ts). A potential drawn above 99 is drawn again (up to six times) instead of landing on 99. Above 70 the peak curve now falls close to a straight line to 100 (the 5-point bands, as a share of 70 to 74: 1, 0.773, 0.569, 0.425, 0.258, 0.082; the line asks 1, 0.818, 0.636, 0.455, 0.273, 0.091). Regular guy only.
Every prospect gets a board score:
55% current OVR, 35% what scouts think his ceiling is, 10% production, minus 1.2 for each year older than 19, plus a little noise.
The order:
a lottery among non-playoff teams for the top four picks (the worst teams have the best odds), then worst record first. Teams pick the best board score, with a little disagreement.
A chance after every game he plays:
base 0.92% × durability (hidden) × the plan × minutes (tired legs) × age (×0.85 under 24, ×1.2 from 30, ×1.4 from 34) × difficulty, more for very tall bodies.
Wear builds up
from minutes and hard plans and raises the risk; recovery plans and rest bring it down.

blocks.text: Legacy and the Hall of Fame

items: Legacy points add up the career:

MVP 9, Finals MVP 5, All-NBA 5/4/3, DPOY 4, a title 3 (4.5 as a key player), All-Star 2, ROY 2, scoring title 2, other stat titles 1.5, Sixth Man 1, 1 for every 1,500 NBA points, an NCAA title or EuroLeague 2.
Hall of Fame:
100 legacy points (about the top 11–13% of Regular guy careers).

blocks.text: How new things change the balance

items: Everything feeds a few levers:
ratings (through growth), minutes, team strength, morale, fame and the body. A new event, plan, stat or feature matters only through these.
Ratings and growth:
a rating bonus from an event counts once; a change to growth (a plan, a culture, a mentor) compounds every half, so small growth changes move peak OVR the most.
Team strength:
one point is roughly five or six points of win chance per game, which the playoffs multiply (see the title table). Features that add strength move titles much more than awards.
Awards are races:
they rank him against the league, so a feature that helps everyone (or the whole league) changes little; one that helps only him moves his award odds.
Minutes:
more minutes mean more stats, more growth and more injury risk at the same time (the deep-bench change is an example).
Roster fit adds team strength only for his team,
so it moves titles more than awards; it was calibrated to add nothing on average, so it changes who wins rather than how often.
Difficulty:
each mode changes potential, growth speed and injury risk, not the league.
That is why every change is checked with the simulation:
thousands of careers are played and compared with the last approved numbers (peak OVR, NBA, All-Star, MVP, Hall of Fame, titles) before it ships.

blocks.text: Round 37’s check of the curve change: 2,000 Regular guy careers on fresh seeds (20000 on), smart policy, casual mini-game play, before and after the settle-back and the redraw. The owner, round 37: “i think the balance is good enough”.

The honours that need a star are rarer because the straight slope has fewer stars than the old hump in the high 80s and 90s. Round 36’s bar run (2,000 careers, before → after): All-Star 36.15% → 30.55%, MVP 13.00% → 9.55%, the Hall of Fame 15.65% → 16.60%, titles 38.30% → 39.30%, mean peak 74.1466 → 74.2029.

blocks.text: Hidden traits rolled at the start

items: Potential and caps:
a hidden ceiling for every rating; the scouting grade is a guess at it that gets more accurate with age.
Growth rate:
hidden, about 0.5x to 2.2x; grind plans, mentors, film sessions and early-morning workouts can raise it.
Growth type:
early 20%, standard 60%, late 20% (early bloomers peak young, late bloomers keep climbing).
Aging profile:
durable 20%, normal 60%, fragile 20%; decline starts at 31 (durable), 29 (normal), 27 (fragile).
Durability:
a hidden injury multiplier (0.7 to 1.3).

220 lb at 6′7″, 6.5 lb per inch taller (less per inch shorter); teenagers carry a share of it and grow into it by 21.

Lighter than best:

better growth and play when high; plans, events, roles, results and cities move it.

from 30, Recovery and Team first grow 8% more, injure 12% less and add 2 trust; Team first also lifts the team 0.2 more.
On the cards:
the plan cards carry the tag, and the edge applies to a main plan or a side plan alike.
Where:

a pixel room on the Season tab, under Extras (fast break folds it away): the starting five, two from the bench, and the head coach at his door. A and D or the arrows walk, Space, Enter or W talks, 1 to 3 answer, Escape leaves; on a phone, buttons. The keys work only while the room has focus.
Characters:

the youngest is the rookie (22 or a rookie contract), the oldest the veteran (30 or more), the best of the rest the star (within 4 OVR of him); the others are a joker, a quiet pro or a hothead, fixed by name. About every other half the hothead starts a feud with someone.
Talks:

once each a half (the halves and the postseason). Each character has two or three answers: mentoring the rookie (chemistry +0.15, trust +1), the veteran’s advice (morale +2, a little longevity), a two-man game with the star (+0.2 when close in OVR), watching film with the quiet pro (Basketball IQ +0.3)... Settling a feud: break it up (+0.25), take a side (−0.1) or stay out (−0.05).
The cap:
the room moves chemistry by 0.6 at most each season, either way (LOCKER.cap).
Firing the coach:
in the NBA, at reputation 90, once a season: a new coach a little better than an average hire, trust 60, chemistry −0.4 straight off the season (past the cap), morale +6, reputation −2.
Who:

every team has one, named from the team and how many coaches it has had (a new man each time one goes), with a temperament and pixel art of his own: the hardliner folds his arms, the tactician holds a clipboard, the players’ coach has his hands together; a suit with a tie in the team colour or a tracksuit, grey hair or glasses on some. He stands in the locker room, the team style talk and a Home card.
Temperament:

a players’ coach: chemistry +0.1, a point of morale a half, trust swings ×0.8. A tactician: +0.15 team strength in the postseason. A hardliner: growth ×1.05 in a half on the grind, trust swings ×1.25, a point of morale less. Listed with the season’s team factors.
The role talk:

once a season while it is on, unless he already has the biggest role. The chance of a yes is 0.3 + 0.012 a point of trust above 50, +0.15 with a players’ coach or −0.1 with a hardliner, +0.15 near the top of the roster, kept between 0.05 and 0.9 (shown only as words). Yes lifts trust to where the role moves up and adds morale +3; no costs trust 3 (6 with a hardliner) and morale 3. Measured: 41.6% yes over 387 asks in 30 test careers.
The hot seat:

when his team is under .400 after 12 games, an event: back him in public (he keeps his job with a chance of 0.25 + 0.005 a point of reputation, and trust +8 if he does), stay out of it (fired 60% of the time) or, at reputation 60, tell the front office it is time (the new coach starts trust at 55, chemistry −0.1, reputation −1). A firing is real: a new name and face, and in the NBA a new coaching factor in team strength.
Coaching changes:
NBA teams under .350 may fire their coach in the offseason (45%); with his own team, trust starts over at 50.
Coach of the Year:

the coach whose team beat its talent by the most (its rank by wins against its rank by strength, among teams at .500 or better). His own coach winning it is trust +3, and a bigger club may then try to hire him away (an event).
The watch:

in the NBA, Home warns when a season could carry him past a legend on the all-time scoring list (each legend’s points per game × seasons × 72 games; the pace is his last NBA season’s points) or when a career high comes within reach of a league single-game record (100 points, 55 rebounds, 30 assists, 11 steals, 17 blocks, 14 threes).
Chasing it:
once a season, for the list: usage ×1.05 and injury minutes ×1.1 for the season, chemistry −0.1. Light by design (owner: “dont make it influence the game too much”).

items: The shop:

223 items on six shelves (Shoes 9, Gear 26, Training 61, Recovery 28, Lifestyle 59, Accessories 40), up to $400M. Six things a visit and no limit on buying: he buys as many as his bank pays for. Prices follow his income (salary plus brand deal): the sticker price up to $1M a year, rising on a log scale to three times it at $50M a year and above (at $10M, ×2.177184), rounded to two figures. The six are drawn around 42% of his bank each (a spread of 0.45 on the log of price over that target), so two or three fit together; from $20M a year that share falls, on a log scale, to 3% at $50M, where all six fit with money to spare. One from each shelf while shelves have something near his price, a second from a shelf otherwise; an accessory is one of the six on 40% of visits (cheap at any income, for the wardrobe); things bought before come up half as often. perfect within 50 ms of the beat, good within 120 ms; a press up to 200 ms early counts the note as missed, so mashing does not pay. The clock is the sound coming out of the speakers, so presses line up with what the player hears.

a run lasts 44.95524 s on average (38.4 to 51.72 s), with 88.2315 notes (54 to 126), 1.962652 notes a second and 7.688 long notes; the longest wait for a note is 2.4 s; all 14 sets appear. A scripted player pressing exactly on the beat scores 100% (all perfect).

drawn in pixels on one 100 by 80 grid: asphalt with a dither, a chain-link fence, the backboard, rim and net, the paint and a stepped arc. It takes about two thirds of the width on a computer.

blocks.text: Music and sound in the mini-games

Each mini-game but Lockdown has a music loop of its own: Front Office (a walking-bass ii–V–I), Rack ’em for the three-point contest, Showtime for the dunk contest, Lab coat, Blacktop for 3-on-3 and Hall of legends; the hub and the daily challenge’s page share Arcade. Lockdown plays its beat instead: four sticks to count in, then a kick on 1 and 3, a snare on 2 and 4 and a hat on every half beat, at one of seven tempos, 100 to 124 beats a minute in steps of four; the fourteen offensive sets are the notes pressed on top of it and make no sound of their own. The three-point contest has a sound for each shot (all net, in off the rim, off the rim, a brick, a money ball), the fire, the last five seconds and the buzzer; the dunk contest a slam, the judges and a miss.
Two kinds: what happened in the mini-game itself, and what its bonus did for a career (chapter Records, achievements and the community).

Every title game, and every final he loses, ends with its last minutes told play by play. A 60-50-90 season, a season under 30% or 36% from the field, 95% from the line and an OVR of 15 never happened in either, so none is in the book; 10 OVR, the owner’s example, is out of reach (the lowest seen was 16.6, a body hanging on past 45).
Simple math, the fundamentals and the pages

items: The arcade (19):

every finished run counts on this device, with or without a career: a first run; every game once; 25 and 100 runs; 20 and 27 in the three-point contest and winning it; winning the dunk contest and a 48+ dunk; winning the Legends showdown, three times; a Front Office title, three in one run; a 90 and a 95 built in the lab; a 3-on-3 rout; an A and an S in Lockdown; the top result in all of them.
In a career (7, with the older Side Quest):

what the claimed bonuses did, kept in the career (miniLog: the game, the season, the OVR and range it added): bonuses from three games, and from all seven, in one career; ten claims; 2 OVR from bonuses; range from the three-point contest; a bonus five summers in a row; an NBA title in a season with a bonus.
Leaderboards:

today and all time, five boards: one for each difficulty, one for Rough Road and one for Comet: the top 100 players, each counted once at their best career (offline, this device’s own best careers). A Rough Road career ranks on Reality’s board and its own; a Comet career only on its own, so the Shoot for the stars board keeps careers played by hand. Online the database files each career on its boards as it is posted (supabase/migrations/0003_challenge_boards.sql: best_all and best_day hold the five boards; the posting function checks the marks match the difficulty). Ranked by the career index. Ten house players stand on each board.
Career index:

built like the JAWS score used for real Hall of Fame cases. Every season is worth its honours (the legacy points of the awards won that year), its NBA points (one per 1,500, playoffs included) and how good he was (a tenth of a point for every OVR above 60 at the end of the season, at any level). The index is the average of the career total and the best five seasons in a row, so a long career and a great peak both count. Measured over 1,000 Regular guy careers (smart choices, casual mini-games): mean 40.1196, median 17.45, top 10% from 117.82, top 1% from 242.247, best 291.3; Hall of Famers average 169.468, MVPs 171.283, All-Stars 89.8216, NBA players who never made an All-Star team 14.0692, careers that never reached the NBA 1.9242. It ranks careers almost exactly as legacy points do (correlation 0.991186) and tracks peak OVR at 0.819274.
Reality 99 hall:
every Reality hits hard career that reaches a shown 99.
Statue plaza:
Regular guy careers with 150+ legacy points can raise a statue (gold from 220, or a first-ballot Hall of Famer; bronze otherwise), 100 at most. Others can open its card and pay respects, once each.
What a career qualifies for:

at the end of a career a note says where it stands: its rank on today’s and the all-time board (against real and house rows), the Reality 99 hall, and a statue (with the button to raise it) or how much legacy it still needs.
Feedback:
a note to the game’s maker that only the maker can read; no address appears anywhere.
Live strip:

players with the game open now, on any page (two tabs in one browser count once), careers ended since you opened it, today’s theme (the daily prospect), and the latest news. The two numbers include house players (simulated, like the house careers on the boards), and the strip says so in its bottom-right corner: about 300 to 1,500 on the court over a day (lowest around 10:00 UTC, highest around 22:00), moving every few seconds, and careers ended rising from the moment the page opens toward a share of the court (35 after five minutes, about 230 after an hour), always below it. The real numbers, without the house players, are in the dev deck’s header.
Where it lives:

the claude.ai page’s shared database (invited contributors can post; everyone else can look). Off that page it falls back to this device. A website with its own database is the other option the owner is weighing.
House players:

so the page is never bare, 36 small careers the game played itself under made-up names (career index 1 to 15, peaks in the 60s, no titles) sit on the boards, ten a difficulty (four of them, changing daily, on today’s boards), and six stand in the plaza in bronze. They are always marked “house”, rank below almost any real career and are never posted anywhere.
Statues:
the cute sprite cast in bronze or gold on a stone plinth with the name.
The Reality 99 hall:

a pixel hall (stone, columns, purple banners, a 99 banner, a carpet) with benches of seated silhouettes, five a bench (three on a phone). A new bench appears once the one above is full; empty seats are locked shadows. A tap lights a seat with a sparkle and pops up the player’s card.

blocks.text: Owner, round 36: “ask the user for a username(changable) after the tutorial. this is for the community function(so that users can know who’s player it is without having constraints on the player name)”. One username a device (src/ui/names.ts), kept under the key Play with friends already used, so a name picked for friends carries over: letters, numbers and _ . -, up to 20, the same swear-word rules as player names.

items: Asked:
on the graduation page; once on the difficulty step for a device that finished the tutorial before (Not now hides it, btr-username-later); changed any time in Settings and on Play with friends.
Shown:

a career posted to the boards, the Reality 99 hall or the statue plaza carries it as by inside the record, so the database needed no migration; the boards, the hall and the plaza show “by” it beside the career, and check it again as they draw, since the server doesn’t. Draft classes’ names follow the same rules. Chat lines between friends stay as typed (owner: “no need for filtering friend chats”).

blocks.text: Owner, round 35: “the theme here is multiplayer”; the owner’s picks: “Draft class with friends, Challenge a friend”, found “both” ways (a code or link, and quick match); “i want the multiplayer under regular guy”. Both are asynchronous: nobody has to be on at the same time.

items: Challenge a friend:

from the last page of a finished Regular guy career, a six-letter code (no I, O, 0 or 1) and a link (#challenge-CODE). A friend plays the same prospect from the same seed and start page, with no undo; when his career ends, his card goes up beside the one that set it, ranked by career index, a player’s best counting. Quick match: others’ challenges from the last 30 days, the least answered first.
Draft class:

up to 12 friends start Regular guy careers on one seed. The class is made or joined as the player starts, its seed his career’s. Each finished season sends a short line (level, team, rating, points, rebounds, assists, record, honours; at most 1.5 KB) and each finished career its card: standings by the best rating so far, then the honours; every season side by side, the best of the class each year marked. Quick match: classes from the last 14 days with a seat left.
Who you are:

the username (see The username above), kept on the device; the game keeps no email or login (the online community’s anonymous secret, of which the database keeps only a hash). A member’s id on a page is a short slice of it.
Its board, beside the career:

owner: “for the multiplayer, a leaderboard should always appear on the side”. A challenge or draft-class career shows its board at the top of Home’s side column and beside every other tab and its last page (sticky on a computer, above the tab on a phone); it never folds, holds this career as it stands now, and refreshes after each season and every minute. Under it: the rival’s record, any classmate on his team, and the chat.
Off the community:

owner: “the career played in multiplayer wont be counted towards the real leaderboards in community”. A career with friends is never posted to the community (boards, feed, statues, the Reality 99 hall); its last page shows its own board instead.
Friends in each other’s careers:

owner: “each user can send a rivalry to one other, and if they accept, they become draft rivals. their dynamics when they meet should be more deliberate. if two users join the same team, they can form duos (or a big three if three are in the same team)”. Each friend’s career is played on his own device, so before each season the side board copies the class’s season lines into the career, and the engine reads only that copy: the same copy gives the same career. A friend is where this year’s line says, or a season behind, where last year’s says.
Rivals and rival nights:

each member picks one classmate from the standings (Send a rivalry, Accept the rivalry, take it back); two who pick each other are rivals. Once a season, when both are in the NBA on different teams, their meeting is a turning point never left to chance: guard him yourself, outscore him, or play it like any other night. The odds start at a half and move 3 points for each point of team strength and 1.2 for each point of OVR between the two, plus 1 or 2 for the call, between 15% and 85%; both players’ points come from their seasons. The last 30 meetings are kept, the record on the side board.
Duos of friends:

a classmate on his NBA team for a season is a duo, two a Big Three, formed the first season of their run together; it counts when the career has no duo or Big Three of its own (or as the third of its own duo), with the usual edge, and a moment marks the season it forms.
The chat:

owner: “try to make a chat below the leaderboard so that the users can communicate”. One for each challenge and each class, under its board, for its people only (a class’s members; a challenge’s maker, the friends who have started it and those who have answered). 200 characters a line, a line every 3 seconds and 300 a day; a room keeps its latest 200 lines and shows 50, polled every 10 seconds.
Fair play:

a prospect from another player is checked before it is played: only what the start page can pick, a rerolled card within six points of its archetype’s in each rating and 320 in all, Regular guy; so a challenge cannot carry a made-up player onto the leaderboards. Posts wait on the device until the server takes them.
Draft night:

owner: “the 12 of you (max) were the first options of your colleges. you’re going for the nba draft, and all of you are predicted to be entering as a 1st round pick (1~30th). ovr starts at a 65~75 range. the rest is history”. A class career skips high school and college: his college’s first option, 19 to 22 (the younger twice as often), OVR 65 to 75 drawn evenly, a mock range in the first round and a pick there (the 30th team takes him if he is still on the board); the whole class in the same draft. Tuned so stars come up about as often as for a first-round pick of a career played from high school (owner: “yes”): over 200 smart careers, mean peak 82.40946, All-Star 69.0%, MVP 9.5%, Hall of Fame 19.5%, against 80.60136, 60.49383%, 9.876543% and 23.45679%.
Fair play:

owner: “for equality purposes, i think sim and fastbreak should be locked in multiplayer. think of other ways to balance”. Fast break and Sim locked off in every career with friends; no mini-game rating bonus; a challenge only from a career that never ran Fast break or Sim; a posted season stands; a class seat holds one career.
Friends in each other’s careers:

rivals (two classmates who pick each other) meet in a rival night once a season, and in a rival series when their teams meet in the playoffs (one call for the series: guard him, outscore him, the team game); classmates on one team form a duo of friends or a Big Three; a classmate shows in the game log against his team, in the award races (he can win MVP) and on the All-Star teams; the trade request can aim at a classmate’s team, the two salaries against the cap setting the odds (not offered past 60% of the cap together).
Reunion night:

owner: “combining them all in reunion night, revealing each of them one at a time ... so class MVP should be last”. Once every career is over (or a friend has been quiet 14 days), eleven awards one at a time: Iron Man, Journeyman, Glass Cleaner, Floor General, Moneybags, Bucket Getter, Highest Peak, All-Star Regular, Hardware, Ring Leader, then the Class MVP; a pixel banquet over it.
The class pages:

tap a friend to watch his career season by season (a pixel chart of his rating, every line, his card); four reactions on a classmate’s season; class news in the chat (drafted, a move, a first All-Star, an MVP, a title, retired), written by the server; and the daily challenge among friends.
Where:

the website and itch.io, on the game’s database (supabase/migrations/0004_multiplayer.sql; 0005 for rivals, takers and the chat; 0006 for 12 seats, fair play, class news, reactions and the daily board): eight tables no player reads or writes directly, nineteen functions that check each write and limit how often it comes (a challenge every 20 seconds and 30 a day, an answer every 10, a class every 20 and 12 a day, a season line every 2 and 600 a day, a rival pick every 5 and 50 a day, a chat line every 3 and 300 a day, a reaction every 1 and 400 a day, a daily run every 5 and 100 a day). The claude.ai page cannot reach that database, so its page points to the website; the dev deck plays on a stand-in on the device, with house players.
Sound and art:

a loop of its own (Call and answer, 132 bpm, two voices taking turns); a pixel pair squared up for a challenge, classmates on a bench under a banner for a draft class; a call-and-answer sting for a challenge and a roll-call bell for a seat taken; two jerseys and a bolt for a rival night; the draft stage for draft night; a toast for each reunion award and a pop for a reaction.
Sending:

a bar at the foot of every tab, tagged with the tab, the difficulty and the age. On claude.ai the page's shared data takes it from the owner and invited contributors, and everyone else gets claude.ai's comment box on the page (composer only); on the website it goes to the game's own database (one note per player every 10 seconds, 20 a day); a copy that reaches neither keeps it on the device.
Reading:

the inbox is a tab of the dev deck, read-only; #inbox opens the dev door and lands on it. On the website it asks once per device for the inbox key, a long random string only the owner holds (the database keeps its SHA-256 and lets nobody else read the notes).

chapters.title: 16. Playing the game: screens, settings, sound and help

items: The visual check:

scripts/visual.cjs opens every dev deck card at desktop and phone width, light and dark, and flags sideways scrolling, clipped or overlapping text, low contrast, small tap targets, script errors, a buried main card and content under the phone's bottom bars; scripts/visual-diff.py lists what changed between runs.
What it found:

the phone Home put four cards above the season's main card; the Records tab was wider than a phone; two lab components shared class names; contrast in gold, warn and badges; small tap targets; an unstyled input.
Navigation:
one page top for the career log, achievements, community and mini-games (Back says where it goes, a you-are-here trail, Escape goes back); tabs open at their top.

blocks.text: Owner, round 37: “can we make the main home page a map as well? ... once the user completes the first tutorial beginner level, they can take a plane to the main land. in the main land, there’s buildings/islands/areas/... where the user can access the main contents”. The start page’s first step is a pixel town along one avenue (src/ui/mainland.ts, screens/MainLand.tsx, art/LandArt.tsx), on a 224 by 100 grid, wide across the page on a computer and scaled to the width on a phone.

items: Above the avenue:

the airport (back to the road map), the cinema (the intro), and a venue for each difficulty: the gym (Regular guy), the cage, a fenced street court under a wall of tags (Reality hits hard, with Rough Road), and the dome under its star (Shoot for the stars, with Comet).
Below it:

his house (Continue, while a career is going; a lot for sale otherwise), the park (Play with friends), the library (the career log), the newsstand (What’s new), the statue plaza (the community), the trophy museum (the achievements), and the dock, with the island of mini-games across the water.
Getting around:

click a place, or drive his car to it with the arrow keys, and its card pops out beside it (under the map on a phone); Tab reaches every place, Enter opens the card where the car is, Escape folds it away. The island’s card sends the boat across with him in it; the airport’s plane takes off before the road map opens.
What it replaced:

the difficulty cards are the venues (Make your player goes on to the Identity step), and the start page’s row of four cards became four places, so there is no row any more. A draft class keeps the old difficulty step.
At night:
in the dark theme a shade over the town, lit windows, lamps and signs, square halos and the dome’s searchlights.

blocks.text: Owner, round 37: “a world to walk around instead of menus”. In a career the row of tabs is a pixel street (src/ui/town.ts, components/Town.tsx, art/TownArt.tsx): the gym is Home, the arena the Season tab, where he lives the Player tab, the hall Records, the arcade Extras; a pro also has an agent’s office, which opens the Player tab at his contract and money.

items: Where:

his hometown in high school (the rec center, his school, the family house, the diner with his clippings), the campus in college, his team’s city as a pro, a city abroad in Europe; a finished career stays on the street of the level he played last.
Walking:

clicking a place opens it at once while he walks to its door; with the town in focus the arrow keys or A and D walk him door to door and Enter goes in; H, S, P, R and E still open the places. Fast break and reduced motion skip the walk. Soft footsteps, and the bell over the door when he goes in.
What it shows:

a banner on the arena for each title won there; his home growing with the bank (a flat, then a house from $3M, a mansion from $40M); his car at the kerb once he bought one as a pro; a hoop by the house once he built a court at home; his statue in gold outside the arena of the team that hung his jersey; a gold dome on the museum once he is in the Hall of Fame; and the turning points’ street sign and mural.
Fitting the screen:

on a narrow screen the street is wider than the screen and follows him; once the town scrolls out of view the row of tabs comes back in the top bar, and a phone keeps its bottom bar. The tutorial levels show only their places; simple text signs show the tab’s name only; night in the dark theme.
Home:

the season’s main card (the choice waiting, or the next step), the player card, How you play (Sim, Fast break, Simple text, Guide, Master, playable playoffs), and Around you: the MVP race, the duo, the rival, the league’s storylines and the fans’ talk in one card, each a tab, opening on what matters most right now (see Around you below). With Sim on, the turning points it decided are listed under the result; a Comet’s highlights under them. Undo sits under the season header (see Undo below). In Simple text, the season’s averages stay in one quiet line above the main card (points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, field goal %: the half so far, the season just ended or the last one).
Season:

the season and the league in one, the most worth a look first: the team, its place, record, streak and form; the playoff bracket while there is one (every series folds out below it); the standings as win bars of pixel cells with each crest and a line after the playoff places, his conference first, beside the team’s strength and its city and fans; the league leaders in points, rebounds and assists as bar charts; his games; last season’s award voting as bars, the last eight champions as their title banners, and the record book.
Player:
ratings, status, kits, scouting, the name card (nickname, logo, brand), Your life (staff, wardrobe and collection as tabs), the Body panel (folded) and the roster.
Records:
the career timeline first, then banners and rings, trophies and totals, career highs and the farewell tour’s gifts; the journal and season by season below.
Extras:

the start page’s four cards inside a career: the mini-games, the career log, the achievement book (with what this career has earned) and the community, under a banner of the mini-games open, what this career earned and the log’s cards and locks. A card lists what the start page keeps while a career is on: the daily challenge, deleting log cards, and starting or continuing another career.
Keys:
H, S, P, R and E switch tabs; the tab bar runs along the top on a computer and the foot on a phone.
Undo:

one step back. Every choice and step on Home, and the offseason moves (focus, recruiting, pay cut, lab, number, contract talks, staff, trade request, position), keeps the game as it was; Undo (or U) puts it back and says what it took back. One step only, and never for Rough Road, Comet, the daily challenge or a career that has ended (canUndo in store.ts), so their boards stay fair. Take Two counts the first.

blocks.text: Owner, round 36: “merge 12”. Home’s side column is one card. Each part shows only when it has something (the MVP race in the NBA near the top, a duo, a rival, the league’s stories, the fans’ talk outside the beginner level), and the card opens on the one that matters most (src/ui/around.ts): a close MVP race (leading it, or within 3) 90, a duo formed this season 85, a rivalry begun this season 80, news about him this season 75, story calls left 65, a race within 6 60, a rivalry that met this season 55, otherwise lower; ties keep the order MVP race, rivalry, duo, the league, the talk. A tab he picks holds until the season moves on. With the tutorial, the closing tour or Guide mode on, every part shows one under another, so each step finds what it points at.

Round 34’s theme was simplification (owner: “for round 34, the theme is simplification. we’re gonna make most in-game cards foldable”). A card with a title folds from it: the title is a button with a pixel chevron (down while open, right while folded), and a folded card is a one-line strip with its name. Cards built by hand (the head coach, the scouting report, How you play, the MVP race, the duo, the rivalry, the fan talk, the locker room, the city and its fans) carry a small tab astride their top edge, so it never covers what the card shows, and fold to a strip with their icon and name. A card with nothing to show leaves no strip.

items: Defaults (the owner’s call):
every card starts open, and a fold stays as it was left on that device, season to season and career to career.
Always open:
the main card, To do, the player card, the offseason moves and the career card.
Keys and sound:
Tab reaches each title and tab, Enter or Space folds; a click sound. A locker room that is folded lets its keys go (its focus leaves with the fold).
Where it is kept:
one list of folded cards on the device; the dev deck keeps its own and deals every card open.
Clicks a season:
measured over 160 smart careers: 13.368080 (a press conference asks one question, two after the biggest stories).
Fast break:
with a test career the five tabs show 15 cards and 1,366 words instead of 41 cards and 6,214 words; the Player tab is 1,216 pixels tall instead of 7,465.
Contrast:

every piece of text on the five tabs, in both themes, was measured against its background (WCAG 4.5:1, 3:1 for large text): the light theme’s orange is a shade deeper (white on it 5.63:1), and gold and amber tags use dark ink. Team badges with letters on them (the bracket’s marks, the champions’ banner) take a readable ink, with the team colour nudged just enough for 4.5:1; the visual check flags anything below AA on every screen.
Keyboard:

every control can be reached with Tab and shows a focus ring; Enter presses the main button, number keys pick a choice (a veteran role card too), letters switch tabs, Escape goes back from a page. The switches are on How you play and in Settings.
Sound:

made in the browser (no files): about 65 effects (clicks, tab switches, pages, tip-off, a new season, a new team, OVR going up, event results, a title fanfare, awards, injuries, fines, coins, a nickname, press cameras, deals, staff, visits, brands, the timing meter, the Rough Road vow and the comet, feedback, retiring, the career log’s padlock, 3-on-3 and the contests, the hall’s reveal and paying respects) and 19 music loops written note by note (ui/tracks.ts) on pulse, triangle and sawtooth waves with a kick, snare and hat: bright ones for the intro (Tip-off, with a Play the music button, since browsers stay quiet until the first click) and the thank-you page (Curtain call), Locker room on the start page, one each for high school, college, the G League, Europe (in waltz time), the leagues around the world and the NBA, Summer league for every offseason and free agency, Jersey night at the end of a career, and one per mini-game but Lockdown. Pages of their own keep the loop under them. Both are on to start (the dev deck starts quiet). Round 35: a loop for Play with friends; effects for a challenge, a seat in a draft class, a mode opening on the road map, a reunion award and a reaction.
The announcer:

the browser’s own speech, the deepest English voice the device has (the natural male voices first, then the classic deep ones) (owner, round 34: “can you find a much more booming one?”): a natural voice keeps its depth (pitch 0.55, rate 0.8), any other goes to the floor (pitch 0.1, rate 0.78); a breath before the big word (“From... downtown!”, “Slam... dunk!”), and under every call the arena: a deep thump, its echo and the crowd swelling. “Blocked!”, “Stolen!”, “From downtown!”, “Buzzer beater!”, dunks, and-ones, alley-oops and posters on the court, a title and a breakthrough on their pages. It follows the sound effects (off with them, at their volume) and has its own switch in Settings. A recorded voice would need a speech engine downloaded into the game, which this round could not do.

blocks.text: The settings menu is in the career’s top bar, on the start page and in the dev deck: theme (auto, light, dark), court background, text size (Normal, Large ×1.15, Extra large ×1.3: every size in the stylesheet follows one multiplier, --ts), sound effects and music each with a volume slider (0–100 in steps of 5, through their own gain on the way to the master; Lockdown’s beat follows the music’s), Simple text, Guide mode and Master mode, the username (outside the tutorial), and in a career Fast break, playable playoffs and New career. Fast break and Sim are locked on for a Comet and off for Rough Road.

items: When:

a step that runs the engine or swaps a whole page (a season half, a choice, a tab, a page, a mini-game) waits one frame so the pop-out is up first; it fades in only if the step runs past a fifth of a second.
What:

your own player in your kit (a playground kid before a career) runs one of nine moves picked at random: dribbling, crossover, through the legs, behind the back, finger spin, two-ball drill, pound dribble, around the world, free-throw routine. Every animation moves only position and opacity, which the browser runs off the main thread, so it keeps moving while the page is busy.

blocks.text: Guide mode (the step-by-step tour, then the next thing to do) starts on for someone with nothing on the device yet: no saved career, career log, achievement or daily challenge, and no say on the switch so far.

Guide mode stays off through the tutorial and the levels, whose own lessons (chapter 2) teach the same things; it is the full game’s help once the road map is done, with a step for Regular guy’s road map card, the fold tab and the Look back bar. Round 35 adds steps for the start page’s locked modes, the book’s categories, Play with friends (its card, the name for friends, its two kinds, the code), Challenge a friend at a career’s end, and in a career with friends its board, the friends in it and the chat; on a class’s page, watching a friend, the reactions and reunion night; the friends’ daily board.
What a tab’s dot was about

A tab with something new since it was last opened carries an orange dot. Opening it takes the page to each change in turn, rings its card and waits for Got it (or Enter): the OVR moving, a new position, a nickname or its logo on the Player tab; new games, a new season or a new NBA champion on the Season tab; new awards, tournaments or seasons on the Records tab; a mini-game that unlocks or an achievement this career earns (named, up to three) on the Extras tab (ui/tabNews.ts, components/TabNews.tsx). The guide’s tour waits while one is up, and Enter or Space on a guide step or one of these presses Got it and nothing else.

items: When:

on every visit, before anything else (owner, round 34: “the intro page should always appear before anything”), and any time from the Intro button on the start page. Start, Enter or Escape goes on. The dev deck skips it.
What:

the title in a 5 by 7 pixel font on a dark plate, over a one-on-one on a full court seen from the side, with side-on pixel hoops at each end: two players about a quarter of the screen tall, always facing each other. Each move is two or three pixel frames: a two-frame run with the ball bounced at the hip, a low reach for a steal, a jump shot, arms-up block and a stand. One dribbles up with the other backing off and reaching in, pulls up over the block and scores through the net; the other takes it back the same way (14 s). The ball is drawn on the players’ own pixel grid, 11 of their pixels across (about nine tenths of a head), with the same dark outline and seams a whole pixel thick. Behind them the court follows a career, five seconds each: a high school gym, a college arena, a streetball court (the easter egg), an overseas arena and the NBA, each dissolving in over the last.

blocks.text: Since round 36 the thank-you is the finale’s last card (see The finale, under Awards and legacy): a finished career plays its ending when it is left, and Play again goes on to the start page.

A Share button sits in the top bar of the career and of the start page, at the top of the community, career log, achievement and mini-game pages, at the foot of every tab and on the thank-you page (a pixel arrow out of a box; on a phone the top-bar button is the icon alone). It opens a pop-up with the game’s link (bench-to-rafters.netlify.app) to copy, the phone’s own share sheet where the browser has one, and links that open a post on X, Reddit, Facebook, WhatsApp or an email. Escape, the X or a tap beside it closes it. The first link sent earns Word of Mouth (a Bench achievement).

A panel that slides in over the right of the start page (a sheet from the foot on a phone) lists the latest changes to the game (content/whatsNew.ts). It opens by itself once after each update for someone who has played on the device before (a first-time player starts on the current version, with the intro and the guide instead); the What’s new button next to Intro opens it again, with a dot until it has been opened. Escape or a click beside it closes it. Changes to how the game plays and looks, not bug fixes.

Report a bug or send feedback, with where it was sent from, sits at the foot of every career tab, every mini-game, the career log and the achievement book; the Developer fold beside it opens the dev deck (with the password) from any page.

Every graphic is pixel art, drawn on a grid with square pixels and hard colour steps: the medals on a 16 × 25 grid, the tab icons 12 × 12, the timeline’s marks and line, the radar built from cells, the charts as rows of cells, and no smooth gradients.

One exception (owner: “for gradient backgrounds (for example, the marraige page background) they can be left unpixelated. it’s actually one of the things i enjoyed before the game”): a gradient behind the art stays smooth: the moment pages, the retirement stage, the position, archetype and lab stages, the glows behind story and duo art, the legend cards, the Hall’s pop-up, the statue plaza, the place backdrops, the lifestyle visit and the thank-you page’s text backing. Meters and objects drawn in CSS (the duo meter, the streetball shot meter, the Hall’s plank, the statue plinth, the courts’ horizons) stay banded.

items: Theme (auto, light, dark), court background (Classic, Hardwood, Streetball), Simple text, Guide mode, Master mode, text size, sound effects and music and their volumes (text size and volumes are shared with the dev deck), up to ten saved careers (each compressed: a 260 KB career is about 64 KB), the daily challenge bests, which tabs were seen, folded panels.
A career code:
Code in the career log turns a whole career into text (see The career code below). Since round 35 only the dev deck can open one.
The road map:

whether the full game is open, the levels passed (and whether each made the goal), the best grade in each island game, the lessons done, the closing tour done, the last level player’s look; and a level career in progress, saved apart from the ten slots.
Folded cards:

the cards folded on this device (round 34), and for the achievement book the most folded at once, the careers looked back on and continued, the road map places opened after the tutorial and the visits.
Play with friends:

the username (btr-mp-name, shared with the community since round 36; btr-username-later once its prompt is put off), a challenge or class link opened before graduation (kept until the page can open it), and posts not yet taken by the server. A career keeps its start (seed and start page) and what it is to friends (a challenge it answers, its draft class, the challenge set from it), with its copy of the classmates’ season lines, its rival and its rival nights and series (the last 30), its run in its class, and whether it ever ran Fast break or Sim.
The road:
a version (round 35), so a device that finished the old tutorial keeps every mode.
Round 36:
which endings have played once (btr-finale-seen), the last Your life tab (btr-life-tab), and the Body panel once opened (open:card:Body, with the folds).
Round 37:

the flight to the main land once seen (btr-plane-seen), and in the device’s career totals the doors he walked through, the agent’s office visits, the feet walked, the landmarks seen and the looks of the town (doors, agentDoors, walked, marks, townRun).

blocks.text: Owner, round 35: “how the import/export code works? is it that a code line is added when the user makes a choice”. No: the code is not a log of choices. Code in the career log takes the whole career as it stands at that moment (the same game state the save slot keeps, every variable in the table above: 396 to 482 KB of JSON for the 12 finished careers measured in round 35), compresses it with gzip and writes it as base64 text after the mark BTR1. and z: (a browser without compression writes the JSON itself, after j:). Those 12 came to 149,803 to 192,599 characters. Making more choices does not grow an old code; pressing Code again makes a new one.

items: Opening one:

the reverse: the text after BTR1. is unpacked and read back as the game state, which opens on its Home as a new career in progress (a fresh save slot). A code that is cut short or changed by hand so that it no longer reads is refused.
Why import is the dev deck’s alone (owner, round 35: “i dont want people abusing the export codes”):

the code is plain packed text with no signature, so anyone who unpacks it could change ratings, honours or money and pack it again, and that career could then post to the leaderboards, the hall and the statue plaza. Since round 35 the import box shows only in the dev deck, and the store refuses an import anywhere else; a career opened there stays in the deck’s own storage, so it never reaches the boards.
What players keep:
Code, on every career in the career log: to send the maker with a bug report, so the career can be opened exactly as it was.

blocks.text: A page for the owner: 167 cards in eight suits, one for every function. A card that needs a career plays one with the balance harness’s smart player until that state appears (a decision, a moment, a stage), then the game opens on it with everything unlocked; it can also play the way the game does (each move, then fast break’s run to the next stop), in sim mode or as a Comet.

items: Where:

inside the game, a card at the foot of the start page (and the foot of every page), behind a password. It opens in place, with no new tab and no reload: the game’s last move is saved, its screen set aside, and the deck’s storage prefix goes on; Back to the game drops anything the deck left waiting, turns the prefix off and puts the game back as it was. The theme, the court and the text size are shared with the game.
What:

the function cards, the Catalog (36 lists with their art, grouped inside each list), Sounds (every effect and the Lockdown beat at each tempo), Music (every loop with the icon of where it plays, one at a time with a stop), this summary, the inbox, and pages of its own: the Action Cam Lab and the loading pop-out’s nine moves (with a button that makes the page lag on purpose).
Settings:
the deck has the settings menu too; its theme and court apply to its own pages.
Reset achievements:

asked twice, empties the game’s own book on the device (achievements and the totals behind them, daily challenges counted again from today) and turns Guide mode back on with its tour from the first step.
Kept apart:
the deck never touches the game’s own achievements, saves or log; scripts/dev-apart.cjs deals every card and checks.
The tutorial:

the Tutorial suit shows the tutorial’s pages on a road of the deck’s own, never saved: the road map early and late and from the start page, each level’s start page, a level career at its first call and in the NBA, beginner’s last shot, a level passed with the goal and without, the island, graduation, a lesson on screen, the closing tour, the start page after graduation and the Skip door. Three of them show their lessons; the deck’s bar stays above the lesson layer.
Round 34:

a card for Home with cards folded, and one for a finished career looked back on (its bar along the top); the road map’s cards press the next place so its card is out; the deck deals every card with every card open.
Round 35:

cards for Play with friends (the page, a challenge, the draft classes, a class, the start page with a class waiting, Challenge a friend at a career’s end, a career with friends on Home and on another tab with its board, a rival night, a duo of friends with the chat, a class on draft night, watching a friend, reunion night before and during, friends today, a class career’s draft-night start) on a stand-in with house players that never touches the real server; the book by category; Iced at the line. Catalog lists for the achievement categories, what the road map opens and play with friends (with rivals, duos of friends, the chat, draft night, the league, the rival series, joining a friend, reunion night, reactions); free-throw touch on items and plans. The game’s store is on window.__deck for end-to-end scripts.
Catalog groups:

inside each list the entries come in groups with a heading: shop items by type, teams by league (the NBA, college, the EuroLeague, high schools by hometown and as opponents, youth academies, each overseas league), events by theme, injuries by severity, archetypes and legends by position, countries by road, levels and overseas leagues apart, awards by kind, looks by part (skin, hair colour, hair, facial hair), house players by difficulty with the house statues apart.
Lists:

besides the game’s content (shop, teams, injuries, events, archetypes, countries, levels, awards, plans, team styles, cultures, nicknames, brands, staff, legends, roles), the Catalog shows the difficulties and their two challenges (Rough Road and Comet, with Comet’s modelled playtime), crunch time’s calls, the music loops (tempo, length, voices), the looks every avatar is built from, the intro’s courts and the house players; the head coaches (each team’s first and the next in line, by temperament), the locker room’s characters with what they say, the league records and the all-time scoring list, and the farewell gifts; the road map’s three levels, the island’s marks, every tutorial lesson, the closing tour’s stops and beginner’s turning points.
